title: I'm making a horde ARPG solo with AI agents driving the Unity editor. Here's what they do and what they don't
author: godstodustgame
selftext:
Solo dev. This is Hekrum, one of nine bosses in the free demo of Gods to Dust, a horde-survival ARPG in the Egyptian underworld. Unity 6, URP.

The honest split. Much of the code is written with Claude Code and Codex, which drive the editor through MCP. The repo's at about 1,800 C# files and 4,900 commits. Voices and some music and sound effects are ElevenLabs, some of the voices made from my own recordings. The story paintings, boss cards and store art come from OpenAI and Google image models. Meshy made a few enemies and some props, scenery and gear, about 560 models next to about 4,800 from purchased packs. Most of what you're looking at in the clip is those packs.

Two things that actually helped. Every agent reads the same rules file in the repo before it touches anything, and whatever it learns goes into the docs, since one agent's memory never reaches the next. And image models drift on a character from words alone, so every painting of a boss or an arena gets renders of the real thing from a few angles.

I play the dev build and hit F11 when something's off, and an agent in the editor picks up the report and fixes it.

The demo's free. Play it and tell me what sucks. If you end up liking it, a wishlist helps a ton. Steam link's in the comments.

replies.author: Gustafssonz
replies.body: Isn't the files in Unity text based? In godot the files are text based, so agents can write scenes and stuff directly without MCP. I'm not sure if this is the best approach thou.

replies.author: godstodustgame
replies.body:
Yeah, Unity’s files are text too (YAML), and the agents do edit them directly sometimes. A boss’s tuning (timings, damage, ranges) lives in a data file, and editing that text is quicker than changing code because Unity doesn’t have to recompile.

Scenes and prefabs are harder though. Every link to another asset is a GUID out of a separate .meta file, objects point at each other by ID numbers, and a prefab placed in a scene only stores what’s different from the original. One wrong ID and something just shows up missing, usually with no error. And if the editor already has the file loaded, it can keep the old values until it’s forced to reimport, so the agent thinks the change worked when it didn’t.

So for me MCP is less about writing files and more about the loop. The agent can compile and read the console errors, place things through Unity’s own API so the references are always valid, then hit play and grab a screenshot to check its own work. Most of the scene wiring is C# setup scripts the agent writes and then runs in the editor. There are a few hundred of them now, and the last big Hekrum pass was one. The nice part is you can run them again and get the same result instead of a pile of hand edits.

From what I’ve seen Godot’s .tscn files are way cleaner, so I can totally see editing them directly working fine there.

comments.author: thecrownforge
comments.body: The F11 report loop sounds useful. How do you check that a fix for one boss doesn't break another one? With nine bosses, I'd want a small repeatable test after each change, then a real play session before calling it done. I'm curious what part of that you automate and what you still check yourself.

replies.author: godstodustgame
replies.body:
Oh man good question -- honestly they're all isolated so the hope is that there's no lingering crossover -- but it's funny you ask that because originally they were a unified boss system and I ran into issues because of that.

Claude's also excellent at testing -- but to answer your question directly I do targeted changes then use my debug panel to portal and test that change. As for spillover or inadvertent changes, I usually do a full run through the entire game (only about an hour or two right now) once a week. But I save that after many edits. So far I haven't seen many unintended changes, but they do happen.

I'm sure once I start scaling the game I'll need to be more diligent and double-checking claude's changes and preventing unnecessary changes across systems.
